The Warm-Up: A Bird’s-Eye View of Our First ODE

Alright, March 30, here we go! We are going to have a lot of props today, but we will do a little bit of writing first to get a bird’s-eye overview of the math we have been tackling over the past couple of weeks.

If you haven’t already, grab a drink—water, Sprite, whatever you prefer. It will become clear in a moment what this drink is for.

For the last couple of weeks, we were doing experiments on exponential decay. I was actually tricking you into learning about the first differential equation of this class. It has a very fancy name: the first-order linear homogeneous differential equation. That sounds intimidating, but let’s break down what it actually means in plain English.

This type of differential equation says that the rate at which “something” is changing over time is exactly equal to a constant rate multiplied by the current amount of that exact same “something”. Mathematically, we write this as:

\begin{equation} \tag{1} \frac{dy}{dt} = r \cdot y \end{equation}

Let’s define our variables:

  • y is our “something”—the quantity we are measuring, which is a function of time, y(t).

  • \frac{dy}{dt} is the time derivative, representing how fast that quantity is changing.

  • r is the constant rate (a decay rate if negative, or a growth rate if positive).

What is this “something”? It should be painfully clear based on your recent lab reports! You measured it: temperature. More specifically, we looked at the temperature deviation, \Delta T = T - T_a (where T_a is the ambient temperature).

But this equation shows up everywhere. What else could be growing or decaying exponentially?

  • Money in a bank account: Earning compound interest (wishful thinking for most of us, but mathematically sound!).

  • Biology: The population of something undesirable, like cockroaches or pathogens, multiplying out of control.

  • Technology: Moore’s Law, describing the number of transistors per chip area doubling over regular intervals.

Visualizing and Checking the Solution

Strictly speaking, the solution to a differential equation is not a single number; it is a function. It is something that has a shape, something you can graph.

If our rate r is negative (r < 0), we have exponential decay, like our temperature deviation cooling down to room temperature. If our rate r is positive (r > 0), we have explosive exponential growth, like a rodent population getting out of hand. In both cases, the function is proportional to an exponential term, e^{rt}.

If you are comfortable with integration, you can solve Equation 1 directly to prove that the solution is an exponential function. But in many other cases, solving differential equations by hand gets really hard. My goal is not to make you grind through the calculus, but to teach you to recognize the standard differential equations you will see over and over in STEM, and to know what their solutions look like.

Even if a random stranger hands you a function and claims it is the solution, you can always do a quick check to see if it is legit. Just like checking your algebra (if x^2 = 4, you plug in x = 2 and x = -2 to verify), we can plug our proposed solution into the differential equation.

Let’s check the function y(t) = e^{rt}. We take the time derivative:

\begin{equation} \tag{2} \frac{d}{dt} \left( e^{rt} \right) = r e^{rt} \end{equation}

Because t is our variable and r is a constant that doesn’t depend on time, the chain rule tells us to pull the constant r out in front and keep the rest of the exponential the same. Look at that! The derivative of the function is just r times the original function. It matches Equation 1 flawlessly. Easy peasy check.

Leveling Up: The Diffusion Equation (PDE)

Now I want us to move on to a second differential equation. It is going to look a lot fancier and mathematically more complicated, but conceptually, it is something you experience every day.

This is the diffusion equation, also known as the heat equation or Fick’s Second Law. If you have taken biology, you might have heard of Fick’s laws in the context of ions diffusing across a cell membrane.

Here is what the diffusion equation looks like:

\begin{equation} \tag{3} \frac{\partial C}{\partial t} = D \frac{\partial^2 C}{\partial x^2} \end{equation}

Let’s unpack this notation, because it looks a bit different from what you saw in first-year calculus.

First, notice the derivative symbol. Instead of the standard lowercase d, I am using the curly Greek letter delta (\partial). Whenever you see this, it means we are dealing with a partial derivative.

Why do we need partial derivatives? In our previous temperature experiment, the temperature deviation was a function of time only, T(t). We fixed the position of our measurement, so we didn’t care about spatial dependence. But with diffusion, we have to keep track of both time and position. You are looking at a spatial profile that evolves over time.

Therefore, our “something” in this equation is a function of two variables: C(x,t).

  • C(x,t) represents concentration or particle count. It depends on position x (where you are looking) and time t (when you are looking).

  • \frac{\partial C}{\partial t} is the first partial derivative with respect to time. It tells us how the concentration at a specific spot is changing as the clock ticks.

  • \frac{\partial^2 C}{\partial x^2} is the second partial derivative with respect to position. It tells us about the curvature or spatial distribution of the concentration.

  • D is the diffusion constant or diffusivity. This is a specific property of your physical system (e.g., the material the particles are moving through).

When we have a function with more than one input variable, and we want to take the derivative with respect to just one of them while holding the others constant, we use the partial derivative \partial. If you know how to take a normal derivative, partial derivatives are not scary at all—you just treat the other variables as constants. And taking the derivative of a partial derivative just gives you a second partial derivative, \frac{\partial^2 C}{\partial x^2}.

Because this equation involves partial derivatives, it is called a Partial Differential Equation (PDE), as opposed to the Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) we looked at earlier.

Where do we see this equation in action?

  • Heat spreading: If you heat one room in a house but leave the rest unheated, the thermal energy will slowly spread out.

  • Biology: Ions diffusing across a concentration gradient.

  • Semiconductors: Electrons diffusing from an area of high electron concentration to an area of lower concentration.

Diffusion vs. Drift: The Kool-Aid Experiment

Let’s do a little experiment. You all have a cup with your drink (water or Sprite). I brought some food coloring and some Kool-Aid powder. Go ahead and put a drop of food coloring or a pinch of Kool-Aid into your cup and observe what happens.

If you used the Kool-Aid, you probably saw the liquid turn red or purple almost instantly. You can see the stuff swirling around as it spreads.

Now, I have a question for you: Is what you are seeing in your cup right now diffusion?

The answer is no.

There is a massive distinction in physics between two types of transport: Diffusion and Drift.

Drift: Directed Motion

What you are observing in your cup is primarily drift (specifically, convection). Drift is motion that is directed by a force or a field. When you drop the food coloring in, several forces take over:

  • Gravity: The food coloring or Kool-Aid powder is slightly denser/heavier than the water, so it sinks to the bottom.

  • Thermal Gradients: There is a fair amount of liquid in your cup. Some areas might be slightly warmer or colder than others, creating convection currents that carry the particles along.

  • Fluid Movement: Just pouring the drink, swirling the cup, or the impact of the drop hitting the surface creates mechanical currents in the fluid.

In nanoscience and semiconductors, we also talk about drift. When electrons move because they are being pushed or pulled by an external battery or a built-in electric field, that is drift. They are drifting along or against the electric field lines.

Diffusion: The Random Walk

Diffusion, on the other hand, is driven entirely by a random walk. It is the statistical result of countless particles randomly bumping into each other (Brownian motion), gradually spreading from areas of high concentration to low concentration without any macroscopic fluid flow or external forces directing them.

I initially thought dropping dye in a cup would be a great, simple diffusion simulation. But it turns out, the more you look into it, the less diffusive it actually is!

To actually observe pure diffusion in a liquid, you have to go to great lengths to eliminate drift. You need a thin container (like a test tube) to stop swirling. You need to keep the temperature strictly uniform to stop thermal convection. You have to isolate the setup from air currents. You even have to use a base liquid (like 5% salt water) that is slightly denser than the dye so the dye floats and doesn’t sink due to gravity.

When you take all those precautions, you discover something incredible: Diffusion is extremely slow on a macroscopic scale.

If you set up a proper diffusion experiment in a test tube, it takes hours and hours just to see the dye move a single centimeter. The math of diffusion tells us that the distance a particle diffuses, x_D, scales with the square root of time: \begin{equation} \tag{4} x_D \sim \sqrt{D \cdot t} \end{equation}

This scaling law has massive implications for biology. Have you ever wondered why cells are so small? Why don’t we have elephant-sized single cells? It is because cells rely on diffusion to obtain oxygen and nutrients. Over a distance of 10 microns (the size of a typical cell), diffusion takes less than a second—it is incredibly efficient. But if a cell were 1 millimeter across, it would take about 40 minutes for oxygen to diffuse to its center. The cell would suffocate! Diffusion is fast on the micro-scale, but agonizingly slow on the macro-scale.

So, scratch the Kool-Aid as a scientific model for diffusion. But hopefully, you are enjoying your drink!

Simulating a Random Walk (In-Class Activity)

Since we can’t sit here for 48 hours watching dye slowly diffuse in a test tube, we are going to simulate diffusion ourselves. We are going to play a game of 1D diffusion using paper and dice to model a random walk.

Get into teams. I want one person to take a sheet of paper and tear it into 16 small squares. Number them 1 through 16. These are our "particles."

While they are doing that, the other teammate will build our 1D diffusive environment. Take another sheet of paper and fold it in half (hotdog or hamburger style, doesn’t matter), then fold it again, and again, until you have a track of distinct slots. Draw lines along the folds to make the boundaries clear. You should start with at least 8 slots in the middle, but leave room to add more slots to the left and right, because our particles are going to spread out.

Place 8 particles in the middle-left slot, and 8 particles in the middle-right slot. This represents a high initial concentration C(x,0) at the center of our space.

The Rules of the Game

The rules for the random walk are simple:

  1. Pick a particle (start with particle 1).

  2. Roll a standard six-sided die.

  3. If you roll an odd number, move that particle one slot to the right.

  4. If you roll an even number, move that particle one slot to the left.

  5. Repeat this for all 16 particles.

Once you have rolled for all 16 particles, that represents one "time step" (\Delta t) in our simulation.

I want you to take a picture with your smartphone after Step 1. Then, go back to particle 1, roll the die again, and move it from its new position. Do this for all 16 particles to complete Step 2, and take another picture.

If we do this enough times, you will see the macroscopic concentration profile C(x,t) naturally emerge from the microscopic random behavior of individual particles. The sharp peak in the center will flatten out and spread wider and wider, exactly as predicted by the PDE in Equation 3.

We only have a few minutes left today, so if you have your paper and particles prepared, keep them safe. Put them in a Ziploc bag or fold them up carefully. We will hit the ground running with this simulation at the start of next class. Have a great afternoon!
